schema_doc: PRD-014 / RFC-017 — surface-hotspot tier metadata sidecar. Joins to moon-sites.json + mars-sites.json by site id. Sites without an entry render Tier 0 only (silhouette via existing moon-lander-models.ts / mars-lander-models.ts dispatcher). Sites with hotspot_tier_max >= 1 get progressive LOD via the hotspot dispatcher. tier2_source paths are provenance-style; the frontend joins them to image-vision.json (Image Pipeline v2 #148 manifest) to find the 1:1 pre-cropped variant URL. Showcase flag = polished editorial treatment (4-6 annotations in S5).

hotspot_annotations.label: Eagle descent stage
hotspot_annotations.explain: The lower half of the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle. It stayed on the Moon when the ascent stage lifted the crew off after the July 1969 landing.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC coordinates + NASA NSSDCA mission page); object unmistakable in the frame

hotspot_annotations.label: Passive seismometer (PSEP)
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Passive Seismic Experiment of the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package, set up south of the Lunar Module on 21 July 1969 to record moonquakes and impacts.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC + NASA NSSDCA; agree on area to ~10 m, pixel from LROC)

hotspot_annotations.label: Laser retroreflector (LRRR)
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Laser Ranging Retroreflector Array left by Apollo 11: a reflector that lets observatories on Earth time laser pulses bounced back from the Moon. Placed about 5 m north-north-west of the seismometer package.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC layer + NASA NSSDCA relative position)

hotspot_annotations.label: US flag (LROC position)
hotspot_annotations.explain: The point LROC's Apollo 11 hardware layer gives for the flag, about 14 m west-north-west of the Lunar Module. The flag itself is too small to see at this resolution.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC coordinates; low: LROC hardware-layer point (no uncertainty given, not in the 2016 table); the flag is not resolvable at 0.4 m/px

hotspot_annotations.label: TV camera (LROC position)
hotspot_annotations.explain: The point LROC's Apollo 11 hardware layer gives for the TV camera, about 26 m north-west of the Lunar Module. Nothing is resolvable in the image at that spot.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC coordinates; low: LROC hardware-layer point (no uncertainty given); nothing resolvable at the point

hotspot_annotations.label: Little West crater
hotspot_annotations.explain: The crater LROC labels Little West on its Apollo 11 map, about 75 m east of the Lunar Module. A faint footpath in the image runs toward it.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC label (Featured Sites nomenclature layer); medium: label point sits on the crater (dark shadowed floor, bright rim) in the image

hotspot_annotations.label: Double crater
hotspot_annotations.explain: A small crater LROC labels Double, about 17 m south-west of the Lunar Module, on its Apollo 11 Featured Sites map.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC label (Featured Sites nomenclature layer); low: label point 17 m south-west of the Lunar Module; a crater is nearby but the ring is not clearly centred on one

hotspot_annotations.label: Footpath toward Little West
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC says the astronaut paths stand out in its image of the Apollo 11 site. This faint line leads east from the Lunar Module toward Little West crater (the dashed outline marks the area, not a point).
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC Apollo 11 traverse layer + visible line in the image; medium: a faint dark line east of the Lunar Module lies inside the ring; centre point of an area about 45 m across

hotspot_annotations.label: LM descent-engine blast zone
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC says the descent engine scoured a bright halo around the landing sites, most likely by blowing the finest particles away from below the engine. At Apollo 11 it shows as a bright zone about 100 m across around the Lunar Module.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC halo description + visible bright halo centred on the LM; medium: the bright halo around the Lunar Module is visible; ring radius 60 m is read off the image (an irregular area, not a circle)

panorama_metadata.caption: Tranquility Base, EVA-1. Buzz Aldrin photographed the LM Eagle and the U.S. flag soon after landing. Visible Hasselblad seams + chromatic stitching at the LM are part of the published mosaic.

panorama_annotations.label: LM Eagle
panorama_annotations.body: Descent stage of the Lunar Module, where Armstrong + Aldrin stood for the EVA.

panorama_annotations.label: U.S. flag
panorama_annotations.body: Planted ~8 m west of the LM. Knocked over by the ascent stage exhaust on lift-off.

panorama_annotations.label: Buzz Aldrin shadow
panorama_annotations.body: Photographer's own shadow in the foreground — Buzz holding the Hasselblad.

hotspot_annotations.label: Intrepid descent stage
hotspot_annotations.explain: The lower half of the Apollo 12 Lunar Module Intrepid, left on the Moon after the November 1969 landing close to the earlier Surveyor 3 probe.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC coordinates + NASA NSSDCA mission page); object unmistakable in the frame

hotspot_annotations.label: ALSEP central station
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Apollo 12 Lunar Surface Experiments Package, deployed on 19 November 1969. Its instruments included a passive seismometer, a magnetometer and a solar wind spectrometer, all wired to the central station.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC + NASA NSSDCA; agree on area to ~16 m, pixel from LROC, hardware cluster visible under the ring)

hotspot_annotations.explain: NASA robotic lander that touched down on 20 April 1967 on the inner slope of a small crater. Apollo 12 landed about 160 m from it in November 1969, and its crew removed about 10 kg of parts, including the TV camera, on 20 November.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC table + LROC labelled image; NSSDCA repeats the LROC coordinates, not independent)

panorama_metadata.caption: The ALSEP site in the Taurus-Littrow valley, EVA-1 (12 December 1972): the experiment package, the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the valley's massifs, Jack Schmitt's colour pan. The last Apollo landing.

panorama_annotations.label: Lunar Roving Vehicle
panorama_annotations.body: The third LRV used on the Moon. Total traverse this mission: 35.7 km — still the record.

hotspot_annotations.label: Viking 2 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: NASA's Viking 2 lander, about 3 m across, which landed in Utopia Planitia on 3 September 1976. It shows as a bright spot with a dark shadow beside it.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE PSP_001501_2280 is this patch's product and states the lander is precisely located in it. The ring sits on the bright spot with a dark shadow, 4 m from the NSSDCA landing coordinate (47.6673 N, 134.2809 E), in the same polygonal-terrain setting as the labelled lander enlargement

hotspot_annotations.label: Spirit lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: The landing platform that carried the Spirit rover to Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004 and stayed behind. The small crater just northwest of it is the one the rover team named Sleepy Hollow.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE PSP_001513_1655 is this patch's product; its caption puts the lander (area B) beside the crater named Sleepy Hollow, to the crater's south-east. The ring sits on the bright lander beside that small crater; the offset of the labelled box from Bonneville Crater predicts the position within ~25 m

hotspot_annotations.label: Sleepy Hollow crater
hotspot_annotations.explain: A small crater less than 20 m across, just northwest of the lander, that the Spirit rover team named Sleepy Hollow. The ring marks its centre.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE PSP_001513_1655 is this patch's product; its caption puts the lander beside the crater Sleepy Hollow, to the crater's south-east. The ring centre (about 11 m west, 6.5 m north of the lander) is read off the patch: a bowl with a shadowed north-west wall, 16-20 m across by eye

panorama_metadata.caption: Spirit's McMurdo panorama, taken from Low Ridge beside Home Plate while the rover sat out the 2006 Martian winter (sols 814–932). Husband Hill on the horizon, the rippled El Dorado dunes at its foot.

hotspot_annotations.label: Lander in Eagle Crater
hotspot_annotations.explain: Opportunity's landing platform, left in Eagle Crater (about 22 m across) after the airbag-cushioned landing of January 2004. In HiRISE it is the bright dot in the dark bowl of the crater.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE ESP_050177_1780 is this patch's product; its caption puts the lander "at the center of the bowl of Eagle Crater". The patch is grayscale, so the airbag colour is not visible; the ring sits on the small bright dot (the lander) at the centre of the dark bowl of the ~22 m bright-rimmed crater (PIA21494 gives 22 m) that the rover tracks lead out of, measured in this product

hotspot_annotations.label: Eagle Crater
hotspot_annotations.explain: The small crater, about 22 m across, in which Opportunity came to rest after its airbag landing in January 2004. The dashed outline shows it at true size; the lander is the bright dot at its centre.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE ESP_050177_1780 is this patch's product; its caption puts the lander "at the center of the bowl of Eagle Crater", and the patch shows the lander at the centre of the one bright-rimmed crater with a dark floor. The 22 m size is the figure already used for the lander ring (PIA21494, not re-read); the dashed circle (radius 11 m) is concentric with the lander ring

panorama_metadata.caption: Opportunity's "Lion King" panorama from the rim of Eagle Crater, sols 58 and 60 — the lander and its airbag marks on the crater floor, the rover's tracks out of the crater, and the plains of Meridiani Planum beyond.

hotspot_annotations.label: Bradbury Landing
hotspot_annotations.explain: Where Curiosity touched down on 6 August 2012, a spot the team named Bradbury Landing. In this HiRISE image, taken on 17 August 2012, the rover is the pair of bright dots in the dark ground scoured by the rockets that lowered it. It has long since driven away.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE ESP_028401_1755 is this patch's product (17 August 2012, 11 days after landing). The rover is the only bright object, a pair of dots, at the centre of the dark landing blast pattern, measured to about 1 m; the HiRISE team's labelled cut-out of the same product shows the same object in the same dark pattern; a pixel-level registration of that cut-out failed (the patch is stretched too differently), so the ring rests on this being the only compact bright object in the 512 m patch (strongest by 36 %, within 1 m of the centre). The patch sits 145 m north of its own georeference so it registers with the CTX mosaic (feature-matched, within 5 m); the mission team's traverse starts 31 m south and 83 m east of the rover

panorama_metadata.caption: Curiosity at Gediz Vallis Channel — the rover's 360° view from sol 4220 after drilling the Mammoth Lakes sample, its 41st on Mars. Robotic arm visible at left, just finished drilling; rover deck on the right; real Martian sky in the upper band; Gediz Vallis channel descending through the centre — first place pure sulfur crystals were ever found on Mars.

panorama_annotations.label: Gediz Vallis channel
panorama_annotations.body: Ancient water-carved channel descending Mt. Sharp's slopes. Curiosity drilled the Mammoth Lakes sample here — first pure sulfur crystals ever found on Mars.

panorama_annotations.label: Robotic arm
panorama_annotations.body: 2 m articulated arm with the drill, brush, and APXS spectrometer — visible at left after completing the Mammoth Lakes drill on this sol.

panorama_annotations.label: Mt. Sharp lower flank
panorama_annotations.body: Layered slopes of Aeolis Mons, the 5 km mountain at the centre of Gale Crater that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014.

hotspot_annotations.label: Perseverance landing point
hotspot_annotations.explain: Where Perseverance touched down on 18 February 2021. In this HiRISE image, taken the next day, the rover is the small bright object with a shadow at the centre, between two bright patches of ground cleared by the rockets that lowered it. It has long since driven away.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE ESP_068294_1985 is this patch's product (19 February 2021, the day after landing). The rover (a small bright object with a shadow between two bright blast zones) was matched to the HiRISE team's labelled cut-out of the same product and sits at the patch centre, measured to about 1 m. The patch sits 205 m north of its own georeference so it registers with the CTX mosaic (feature-matched, within 5 m); the mission team's traverse starts 14 m south and 47 m west of the rover

panorama_metadata.caption: First 360° panorama from Perseverance — three days after landing. The rover deck dominates the foreground; Jezero crater floor + the distant rim are visible above the horizon; real Martian sky in the upper bands.

panorama_annotations.label: Mastcam-Z mast
panorama_annotations.body: The 2 m camera mast — the rover's own "eyes" — visible in the centre because the panorama wraps around it.

panorama_annotations.label: Jezero crater rim
panorama_annotations.body: The crater wall ~2 km away; ancient delta deposits are visible at this rim's western edge — the science target Perseverance drove toward over its first year.

panorama_annotations.label: Rover deck
panorama_annotations.body: Foreground of every Mastcam-Z 360° — solar-panel-style deck, sample-tube cache visible at right.

hotspot_annotations.label: Phoenix lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: NASA's Phoenix lander, which touched down on 25 May 2008. It shows as a bright dot in the middle of the dark ground its descent engines blasted; this image was taken 22 hours after landing.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE PSP_008591_2485 is this patch's product (Phoenix hardware, 22 hours after landing); its labelled cutout shows the lander as a bright dot with a dark blast halo. The ring sits on the compact bright dot at the centre of the halo nearest the published landing position; heat shield and backshell are outside the 512 m patch

hotspot_annotations.label: Heat shield impact
hotspot_annotations.explain: Where Phoenix's heat shield hit the ground, about 190 m east-south-east of the lander: a dark patch of disturbed ground where it struck and bounced.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE PSP_008591_2485 is this patch's product; its caption describes the heat shield as a dark marking, disturbance of the ground from impact and bouncing. Matched to the dark blob with a tail by the lander-to-parachute geometry in its cut-outs (distance ratio 1.6 in the raster against 1.9 in the cut-out, angle 44 against 39 degrees); position measured in the north-up patch (172 m east, 87 m south of the lander)

hotspot_annotations.label: InSight lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: NASA's InSight lander, about 6 m wide with its solar arrays out. Its descent rockets blasted the ground around it, leaving the dark patch.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE ESP_058005_1845 (11 Dec 2018, a different product of the same static lander) labels the lander at the centre of a dark halo. The two products were registered on the terrain (cross-correlation 0.51); that offset carries the labelled lander to the ring within ~10 m, and both products show the same bright pair with a dark spot at the centre of a dark halo (fainter in 2025). Not a same-product label

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 16 descent stage
hotspot_annotations.explain: The lower half of the Soviet Luna 16 lander, left on Mare Fecunditatis after the sample-return capsule lifted off on 21 September 1970 with about 101 grams of soil.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: one source (LROC Luna 16 featured image text + LROC Featured Site frame M141899500L whose feature pixel is the crop centre); object unmistakable: bright body with dark shadow in a blast halo

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 17 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Luna 17 lander that delivered Lunokhod 1 to Mare Imbrium on 17 November 1970. Its descent engines brightened the surface around it, which makes the rover tracks circling the lander stand out.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC lander coordinate layer + LROC "Lunokhod 1 Revisited" text describing the lander with tracks circling it); LROC does not annotate this frame, identification by eye from the matching tracks-around-lander pattern

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 17 blast zone
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC says the surface around Luna 17 was brightened by the exhaust of its descent engines, which makes the rover tracks stand out near the lander.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC post 402 text + visible bright halo; high: bright halo around the lander lies under the ring (radius 25 m by eye)

hotspot_annotations.label: Lunokhod 1 tracks
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC points out the Lunokhod 1 tracks starting at the ramps on the east side of the lander and circling it. Lunokhod 1 later drove 10.5 km (the dashed outline marks the area).
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC posts 402 / 11 text + visible tracks; high: dark loops and tracks around the lander lie under the ring (area about 40 m across)

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 21 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Luna 21 lander that delivered Lunokhod 2 to Le Monnier crater on 15 January 1973. Its descent engines scoured a bright zone 10 to 20 m wide around it, and the rover tracks lead away from it.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC "Luna 21 Lander" featured image of this very frame M122007650L + LROC lander coordinate layer); bright body with dark shadow inside the blast zone

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 21 blast zone
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC says the descent engine made a bright zone extending out some 10 to 20 m around the Luna 21 lander.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC post 15 text + visible bright zone; high: the bright zone west of the lander lies under the ring (radius 16 m by eye)

hotspot_annotations.label: Luna 24 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Luna 24 lander on the rim of a crater in Mare Crisium. The August 1976 mission drilled over 2 m into the regolith and returned about 170 grams of it.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: one source (LROC Soviet sample-return post, Luna 24 NAC frames; no coordinate or arrow for this frame); bright specks and dark shadow at the crop centre on the rim of a 64 m crater

hotspot_annotations.label: 60 m crater at Luna 24
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC describes Luna 24 sitting on the edge of a crater 60 m across. The lander is on its north-west rim.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC post 9 text + crater centre by eye (no coordinate); medium: the lander is at the north-west rim of a crater about 55-60 m across; ring at the visible crater centre

panorama_metadata.caption: First Mars soft landing — 14.5 seconds of transmitted scan data before signal lost. There is no Tier-3 panorama to render at this site (yet); the experience here is the honest-historical-artifact framing of the original fragment via the Tier-2 CTX context.

hotspot_annotations.label: Chang'e 3 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: China's Chang'e 3 lander, which touched down in Mare Imbrium on 14 December 2013, the first lunar landing since 1976. The ring marks the lander's site at the centre of this patch; a bright dot without a shadow sits there, and LROC does not say which pixel is the lander.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC's lander coordinate (44.1214 N, 340.4884 E), which is the centre of this patch; moved there from a bright dot with a long shadow 48 m north that an earlier pass matched by pattern. A second bright dot without a shadow sits on the centre; LROC's text (post 637) gives no pixel position for the lander. Medium confidence

hotspot_annotations.label: 450 m crater west of lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC says Chang'e 3 landed about 60 m east of the rim of a 450 m crater, 40 m deep, on a thick deposit of volcanic material.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC post 637 text (rim 60 m west of the lander, diameter 450 m) + crater centre by eye; medium: bright inner east wall and dark floor visible at the position; centre derived, not an LROC coordinate

hotspot_annotations.label: Chang'e 3 blast zone
hotspot_annotations.explain: LROC imaged the site before and after landing and measured the engine blast zone; the diffuse zone reaches 40 to 50 m north-south and 10 to 15 m east-west beyond the brighter focused zone.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: LROC post 929 text; centred on the lander ring (not visible at this Sun angle); low: elongated roughly north-south; not distinguishable at 78 deg incidence, so the ring cannot be checked against the image

hotspot_annotations.label: Chang'e 4 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: China's Chang'e 4 lander, which made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon on 3 January 2019, in Von Kármán crater. The bright ground around it was swept by its landing engine.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC lander coordinate layer + LROC Featured Sites frame M1311886645); the lander's shadow inside a bright blast zone sits at the layer position

hotspot_annotations.label: Yutu-2 rover
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Yutu-2 rover as it was on 7 May 2019, four months after landing, about 120 m west of the lander at the end of its first tracks. It has driven far from here since.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC rover-position layer for this exact frame + the dark rover with a white highlight at the end of the track in the image, 12 m from the layer point)

panorama_metadata.caption: First panorama ever transmitted from the lunar farside. Von Kármán crater within South Pole–Aitken Basin. Yutu-2 rover visible mid-distance; lander shadow lower-left.

panorama_annotations.label: Yutu-2 rover
panorama_annotations.body: First rover on the lunar farside; still operational at 5+ years (the record for any lunar rover).

panorama_annotations.label: Von Kármán crater rim
panorama_annotations.body: Inner rim of the 180 km crater inside the South Pole–Aitken Basin — the Moon's largest, oldest impact structure.

panorama_annotations.label: Chang'e 4 lander shadow
panorama_annotations.body: The lander's own shadow on the regolith — captured by its onboard terrain camera.

hotspot_annotations.label: Chang'e 5 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: China's Chang'e 5 lander in Oceanus Procellarum, imaged by LRO the day after its 1 December 2020 touchdown. The sample-return mission brought back about 1.7 kg of lunar soil.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC 'First Look: Chang'e 5': 'The lander is the bright spot in the center of the outline' + the label drawn on this image; LROC-computed coordinates 43.0576 N, 308.0839 E +/-20 m)

hotspot_annotations.label: Chang'e 6 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: China's Chang'e 6 lander on the far side, in the Apollo basin, imaged by LRO about a week after its 1 June 2024 landing. The brighter ground around it was disturbed by the landing engine.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: one source (LROC 'First Look: Chang'e 6': 'The lander is seen as the small cluster of bright pixels in the center of the image', on the rim of an eroded ~50 m crater; coordinates 41.6385 S, 206.0148 E +/-30 m)

hotspot_annotations.label: Tianwen-1 lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: The Tianwen-1 lander, at the centre of the pattern its descent engines blasted into the dust. The Zhurong rover drove off it after the 14 May 2021 landing.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: medium-high: HiRISE ESP_069665_2055 (6 June 2021, a different product of the same static lander) labels the lander at the centre of its blast pattern; the two products were set side by side at the same coordinates and show the same bow-tie of two bright streaks, the same crater to the south-east and the same bright crescents (terrain cross-correlation 0.64). Not a same-product label

hotspot_annotations.label: Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: India's Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander, which touched down on 23 August 2023 about 600 km from the south pole. LRO imaged it four days later; the bright halo is regolith disturbed by the rocket plume.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC post: 'Chandrayaan-3 lander is in the center of the image, its dark shadow is visible against the bright halo'; LROC coordinates 69.3741 S, 32.32 E)

panorama_metadata.caption: Shiv Shakti Point — first panorama from the lunar south pole. Vikram lander shadow visible foreground; Pragyan rover deployed onto the regolith shortly after this image.

panorama_annotations.label: Pragyan rover (deployed sol +1)
panorama_annotations.body: 26 kg six-wheeled rover. Deployed via Vikram's ramp the day after landing; operated until lunar nightfall (~14 Earth days).

panorama_annotations.label: South pole crater rim
panorama_annotations.body: First successful soft-landing this close to the lunar south pole — water-ice prospect zone.

hotspot_annotations.label: SLIM lander
hotspot_annotations.explain: JAXA's SLIM lander, which landed on 19 January 2024 near Shioli crater. LRO imaged it five days later; a faint change in brightness around it marks where the engine exhaust swept the surface.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC post: 'The SLIM lander on the lunar surface (13.3160 S, 25.2510 E)' + the arrow drawn on this image)

hotspot_annotations.label: Beresheet impact smudge
hotspot_annotations.explain: The dark smudge where the Israeli Beresheet lander crashed on 11 April 2019 in Mare Serenitatis. It hit at a low angle, from the north, about 1000 m/s faster than planned; the smudge is about 10 m across and lowers the surface brightness by about 10%.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: two sources (LROC post: dark elongated 'smudge' about 10 m across at 32.5956 N, 19.3496 E, 95% interval 20 m x 8 m + the box drawn on this image)

hotspot_annotations.label: Backshell and parachute
hotspot_annotations.explain: The parachute and, just south of it, the 2.4 m backshell of ESA's Schiaparelli lander. Both separated as planned before the lander crashed on 19 October 2016. The parachute is many times brighter than the ground around it.
hotspot_annotations.confidence: high: HiRISE ESP_048120_1780 is this patch's product and its caption places the parachute and the 2.4 m backshell south of it at lower left; the parachute crescent with the round backshell just south of it matches the released cutout shape for shape

panorama_metadata.caption: Vandenberg SLC-4E (Falcon 9) and SLC-4W from the air — an aerial view, not a ground-level panorama.

panorama_metadata.caption: Baikonur Site 31/6 from the top of the Soyuz service structure — the pad flame trench below, the steppe and the Zenit facility on the horizon.
